fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. The Teacher says "Everything is futile!" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). He doesn't say some things or a few things. He says everything, and he opens with "Futility of futilities…" It's a big opening line, and it sets up everything else he looks at.

That's it, friend. The Teacher says, "Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." (Ecclesiastes 1:4). People come and go, and the earth remains. It's like a batch of cookies: a whole crowd shows up, the plate empties, everybody leaves, and the plate is still sitting there.

Good guess, but that's not the word. The Teacher says, "Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." (Ecclesiastes 1:4). The generations are the ones coming and going. The earth is the one that remains.

That sounds nice, but the verse has no rest in it. The Teacher says the sun rises and sets, and then it "…hurries back to where it rises." (Ecclesiastes 1:5). The verse doesn't mention any waiting around. It goes straight back to the start, friend.

Yes, friend. The Teacher says, "to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow." (Ecclesiastes 1:7). The water goes right back to where it started, and then it all begins again. That's a commute with no weekend, and I thought my old drawer days were repetitive.

That's it, friend. The Teacher says, "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing." (Ecclesiastes 1:8). You can look and listen all day, and they still want more. It's like scrolling your phone at midnight, saying "just one more," and somehow it's 2 a.m.

You got it, friend. The Teacher says, "there is nothing new under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 1:9). What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again. It's like getting a "brand new" idea in the shower and then finding out you had the same one last year.
